/news/2026/nov/09/russell-brand-sentence.headline: Judge praises bravery of Russell Brand's victims as he is jailed
/news/2026/nov/09/russell-brand-sentence.bodyHtml:
Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday after a judge praised his victims’ bravery and accused him of living “unhindered by the rules by which decent people live”.

As the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, sentenced Brand for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others, he said he had told the trial “a series of lies”. The disgraced comedian had displayed a “casual, arrogant disregard of any woman’s right to say no”, he said.

“About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous. You were clever – and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator,” the judge said.

“Whatever women wear, wherever they go, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and demand justice in the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Mr Brand, act without their consent.”

Brand’s sentencing, the culmination of a four-week trial at Southwark crown court, came after the four women described the impact of his crimes on their lives in victim impact statements. A woman who was raped by Brand said the attack had had lasting consequences.

“Even now, I feel that I am living with the trauma of what happened,” she said. “It is something I carry with me every day and it often feels never-ending.”

Brand, 51, appeared emotionless as he was jailed, but told his wife, Laura: “We’ll be OK,” as he was taken downstairs by the dock officers. His wife replied: “I love you,” before leaving the court in tears.

The disgraced comedian was convicted on Thursday of raping a 21-year-old fan and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.

After his convictions, the Metropolitan police revealed that Brand was under investigation over two further rape allegations.

On Monday, the judge praised the bravery of the women in the case. He also criticised Brand’s “staggering arrogance” before sentencing him to 10-and-a-half years in prison.

In his sentencing remarks, which were broadcast live, Bennathan told Brand: “I pause to pay tribute to the determination and bravery of all the women whose evidence I have been recounting. I do not increase your punishment because of it, but all those women had to face being confronted and being told they had lied, or twisted the truth and, or, they had agreed to your sexual demands: that was all done because of you, on your instructions.”

The judge said Brand had felt “entitled” to grab the breasts of his earliest victim, an MTV worker, at a birthday party in Soho, London, in 2004, because she had wanted to be introduced to him.

“In your trial you said you had never touched a woman sexually without her consent, and that included this woman. In the light of the jury’s verdicts, that was one of a series of lies you told,” the judge said.

The woman told the court that she was “extremely upset and traumatised” and felt “vulnerable” after the assault.

“There were many times I felt visibly sick at the sight of him parading around thinking he can get away with anything,” she said in her statement.

Brand’s second victim told the court that he had laughed after “mauling” her by squeezing her breasts and kissing her sloppily while she was working at the radio station Choice FM in 2005. She said he overpowered her during the “violent” and “frenzied” attack, which took place in front of his entourage.

The judge said: “No doubt your companions thought it was outrageous laddish behaviour that only you could get away with. It was outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal sexual offence, and as it turns out you haven’t got away with it.”

The judge said Brand was happy to exploit the fact that his youngest victim was a fan and showed his contempt for her by storing her number alongside the letter T for “tart”.

The woman told the court she had felt “anxious, humiliated and overwhelmed” after Brand anally raped her without a condom at his London townhouse. She was 21 when Brand picked her from a crowd after one of his performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009.

“I struggled to eat and sleep, and I found it difficult to cope with my emotions. The impact was so significant that I had to take time away from work, and for a period I returned to live with my parents because I did not feel safe,” she said in a victim impact statement.

The judge’s said Brand’s final offence showed his “staggering arrogance” and how his entourage indulged his “dreadful behaviour”.

Brand sexually assaulted the woman in front of his entourage during a recording project at Channel 4 in 2009 when he placed his head in her lap after she was forced to give him a massage.

The judge said: “The whole episode reeks of casual disrespect and your belief that fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live.”

Earlier Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, said the former TV personality was a “fundamentally different person today” and was not “in general terms, a rapist”.

In his submissions, he claimed: “This should be regarded as a man who went too far and overrode consent that had been given.”

There was also a submission in support of Brand from Andrew Sachs’s granddaughter, Georgina Baillie. She was at the centre of a 2008 scandal when Brand and Jonathan Ross put out a Radio 2 segment in which they left Sachs a voicemail claiming that she had been sleeping with Brand.

Winter said Baillie was among six people submitting character references, and said she had been sober for the last six years, and Brand supported her and paid for her to go into rehab for alcohol addiction.

Winter also told the court that Brand’s wife was standing by him before adding: “I’m afraid words are completely inadequate to truly try to convey to your lordship the total devastation she’s experiencing.

“Currently [they] are wrestling with how to exactly explain to a child who’s just turned 10 what has happened here.”

But in his remarks, the judge told Brand: “I am also very conscious that your imprisonment will deprive your children of the presence of their father: that sad loss to them, however, is caused by your serious offending.”

/technology/2026/nov/09/nvidia-jensen-hu.headline: Nvidia's board launches investigation into Jensen Huang's conduct
/technology/2026/nov/09/nvidia-jensen-hu.bodyHtml:
Nvidia has opened an internal investigation into its chief executive, Jensen Huang, over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, as Donald Trump, Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls rally in support of the embattled Nvidia boss.

Trump said he has spoken to Huang on Monday as the scandal reverberated across Silicon Valley and the Nvidia CEO faced an uncertain future.

“I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said: ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him,” Trump said during a White House briefing.

Trump said that the Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI) was “looking into” the issue, but provided few details. “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” Trump said.

The remarks came after Trump threw his support behind Huang over the weekend, telling reporters on Sunday: “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on. I’m sure, I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job.”

“I think he’s an honorable guy,” Trump added, saying he believed that Huang would and should stay on as CEO.

Huang’s defenders framed his affair as a personal lapse in judgment rather than evidence of treachery against the US, which has imposed strict limits on what chips Nvidia can sell to China.

Huang, who has been married to his wife, Lori, since 1985, admitted in an email to employees on Sunday that he had an affair and that he would cooperate with an internal investigation. Nvidia’s board of directors put out a statement the same day that the company was launching a probe regarding reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

The chip mogul is alleged to have had a relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman that US intelligence services suspect of spying for the Chinese government, according to the New York Times. Trump was reportedly briefed on the relationship last year, the Times reported, but took no action. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are unrelated, with the latter being one of the world’s richest men and CEO of Nvidia, worth more than $4tn, for the past 33 years.

US intelligence agencies believe Alice Huang, acting on behalf of Beijing, pushed Jensen Huang to lobby Trump for relaxed export controls on Nvidia’s sales in China, which he has done multiple times publicly. Nvidia said in a statement that neither trade secrets nor US national security had been compromised.

The affair and alleged intelligence operation involving Huang could have far reaching implications for Nvidia and the tech industry, which are already enduring a period of high market volatility. Huang’s leadership of Nvidia, which is deeply financially intertwined with other leading tech companies like OpenAI, has long been viewed as crucial to the company’s success and stability.

As news of the scandal broke over the weekend, Musk and prominent investors shared their support of Huang. Musk posted “I agree” in response to prominent venture capitalist Shaun Maguire’s defense of Huang. Maguire argued the Nvidia CEO “did something incredibly dumb” but that he is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation”.

“Two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” Maguire posted.

“Let’s also not nuke our AI industry because China ran a successful intel op,” Maguire added in a separate post.

Bill Ackman, the US hedge fund manager and pro-Trump billionaire, meanwhile, suggested that Huang is “human” and deserves public support over the affair.

“He is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes,” Ackman posted. “He takes full responsibility as he should. We should all support him and his family. Onward.”

Ackman followed up with another post later clarifying that he wasn’t suggesting Huang “gets a free pass” but that he was “hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security”.

China has meanwhile denied allegations of an intelligence operation targeting Huang, with the Associated Press reporting that foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun rejected the allegations as “entirely baseless vilification and smearing”.

Nvidia and its chips have been an integral part of the AI boom in recent years, with hundreds of billions of dollars committed to building out projects such as datacenters and chip factories. In August, Nvidia agreed to provide a $105bn guarantee to help OpenAI lease an Ohio datacenter.

As Nvidia has grown in prominence, Huang has also become one of the world’s richest people and most influential figures in tech. He has taken calls from Trump in the middle of an all-hands company meeting and on stage at a conference, and attended state dinners with the president and accompanied him on a trip to China. Huang has also been a powerful voice on tech policy, weighing in on issues such as export controls of chips to China and regulation of open-source AI models.

Nvidia’s stock price fell on Monday as speculation swirled around the extent of damage from the affair. Shares of Nvidia, the second-most valuable company in the world, tumbled 4.2 per cent and closed at their lowest level since 7 April as investors questioned Huang’s future.

Agencies contributed reporting

/us-news/2026/nov/09/pete-hegseth-impeac.headline: Bipartisan impeachment push against Hegseth gains momentum in Congress
/us-news/2026/nov/09/pete-hegseth-impeac.bodyHtml:
A Republican lawmaker has moved to force a vote to impeach Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, setting the stage for a showdown over one of the most divisive figures inside Donald Trump’s administration.

Republicans retain control of the House until new members are seated in January, but House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York – widely expected to ascend to speaker – has said he is a “hard yes” on impeaching Hegseth. “Hegseth has got to go,” Jeffries told ABC News on Sunday.

Thomas Massie, of Kentucky, introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing him of illegally waging war without congressional authorization and abusing his powers.

Massie, an outgoing Republican congressman from Kentucky and vocal critic of the president, argued from the well of the House of Representatives that Hegseth had committed “high crimes and misdemeanors” and “has executed unlawful orders” in office.

Massie is expected to have some Republican support for a vote on articles of impeachment. Under House rules, the vote would have to occur no later than Wednesday.

Massie first introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on 15 September, but House speaker Mike Johnson called US Congress into recess before it could be heard.

Hegseth spent the morning on Monday at the Naval War college, announcing an array of changes to military education that he said would enable US military officers “to wage war with such devastating speed, precision and lethality that no adversary dares test American result that’s deterrence – and if they do that, they are completely and utterly destroyed: that we achieve victory”.

But it is the failure to deliver victory that has placed a target on Hegseth’s back.

Trump, vice-president JD Vance and other Republican leaders quickly attributed last week’s historic US midterm election losses by Republicans to the Iran war and its pocketbook effects on otherwise-conservative voters.

Hegseth fired back at his critics in a short video released on Thursday, describing the threat of his impeachment as “all about the politics of personal destruction”, insisting that it “won’t work with me”.

Watchdogs Common Cause and Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington argued that the video is a violation of the Hatch Act, which bars the use of government funds for partisan political purposes.

Massie’s impeachment resolution holds that Hegseth has subverted the power of Congress to declare war with unauthorized attacks on Iran and Yemen; systemically violated laws meant to minimize civilian casualties with the killing of more than 100 children at a school in Iran; and engaged in extrajudicial killings when ordering suspected drug boats in the Caribbean to be sunk and their crews left without rescue.

The resolution also argues that Hegseth’s investigation and threatened prosecution of Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat, and others for calling for troops to disobey illegal orders was an unconstitutional violation of the first amendment, and alleges that the kidnapping of President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela was illegal and unconstitutional.

/environment/2026/nov/10/slight-fall-in-.headline: Rise of renewables and electric cars pushes fossil-fuel emissions into rare fall
/environment/2026/nov/10/slight-fall-in-.bodyHtml:
Soaring oil and gas prices in the wake of the war in Iran have pushed people to look beyond fossil fuels, easing the rise in climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.

Carbon dioxide from oil, gas and coal is forecast to flatline in 2026, according to a comprehensive assessment by scientists based on data from the year so far. Emissions from burning oil alone are set to drop by 2 per cent, as drivers economise on fuel and switch to electric vehicles instead.

The findings, presented on Tuesday morning at the Cop31 climate talks hosted by Turkey in Antalya, show both the impact of the Iran war and the global expansion of cheap renewable energy, chiefly solar and wind power.

Talk of a global turnaround would be premature, however, the report's authors and other analysts said. The reduction in emissions from fossil fuels for 2026 will be about 0.4 per cent compared with last year.

Yet this year's slight fall could be temporary, and was more than offset by increased emissions from deforestation and land use change, following major fires in south-east Asia and further conversions of wild land to agriculture.

Many factors could disrupt the fragile trend of slowing emissions from fossil fuels, including an intensified expansion of coal in India, an easing of oil prices and US president Donald Trump's enthusiasm for fossil fuels. Much greater investment in renewable energy, and low-carbon technology such as electric vehicles, would still be required to make permanent reductions in annual emissions, the report's authors said.

Glen Peters, research professor at the Cicero Centre for International Climate Research, said: "A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak, unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles are pushing emissions down in dozens of countries, and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions."

About 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 will be emitted this year, according to the Global Carbon Budget, an annual assessment by scientists from scores of universities and science institutions around the world, published in the journal Earth System Science Data.

Energy demand continues to increase around the world, as more people gain access to electricity and are pulled out of poverty, but two-thirds of the increase is being met from rising generation from the sun and wind and the uptake of electric vehicles.

However, emissions from deforestation and the conversion of land to agriculture have also ticked upward this year, meaning total carbon emissions are on course to rise slightly for the year, from 42.8bn tonnes last year to a forecast 43.3bn in 2026.

The scientists warned that the world's remaining "carbon budget" – the amount of carbon that can be poured into the atmosphere before global heating is likely to permanently exceed 1.5C above pre-industrial levels – was about 150bn tonnes, or less than four years at current rates.

Already, temperatures have exceeded the 1.5C threshold for more than two years, and El Niño conditions are heating the sea and air further. Global emissions must peak imminently and fall rapidly in subsequent years if the world is to have a chance of limiting the "overshoot" of temperatures above 1.5C.

China, the world's biggest emitter of greenhouse gases, is likely to reduce its carbon output by close to 1 per cent this year, mostly because of a 5 per cent reduction in oil use, following the Iran war. Peters said: "China has had flat emissions for the last few years after a fairly steep increase in the last decade. There's been a lot of discussion about whether China has peaked or not. Whether this is just a one-off and China rebounds next year, we'll have to wait and see, it's too early to say."

India's emissions have grown strongly, mostly from an increase in coal use, while the country's oil use has declined slightly. Emissions from the US are likely to fall by about 1.3 per cent this year, as less coal is used, despite Trump's attempts to boost it.

Bill Hare, chief executive of Climate Analytics, who was not involved in the research, cautioned against taking too much from the report. "The picture from the Global Carbon Budget is a flatline, not a decline – a projected fall of just 0.4% in 2026, a figure that is unfortunately statistically indistinguishable from zero," he said. "We are heading towards a sustained breach of 1.5C by around 2030. With imminent overshoot, we are entitled to expect governments everywhere to move decisively to cut fossil fuel CO2 emissions."

There seemed little sign of such a decisive move at Cop31, where more than 90 heads of state and government, and high-level representatives from more than 190 countries are gathering for a fortnight of talks on the climate crisis.

Hare said: "We see governments in countries such as Canada, the US and New Zealand rolling back climate policies as fast as they can, and countries such as Australia – co-president of Cop31 – continuing to press forward with massive coal and gas developments that are holding fossil fuel CO2 emissions at record levels. There is little sign yet that the Turkish and Australian leadership [of Cop31] intends to build on [the commitment to transition away from fossil fuels made three years ago] with stronger action."

/technology/2026/nov/09/revealed-palanti.headline: Doctors and watchdogs resist Palantir's push into NHS GP records, FOI documents show
/technology/2026/nov/09/revealed-palanti.bodyHtml:
Doctors and data-protection campaigners are pushing back after documents revealed Palantir lobbied a health minister to extend its AI technology into GP records, a stretch of its NHS reach that doctors worry could undermine patients' trust.

The US company, co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel, used a direct WhatsApp channel to argue that "the logic of joining up primary and secondary [care] data is unarguable" and said its software was "ideal" for the job. The push came in February this year despite GP data being expressly ruled out of the scope of Palantir's existing £330m contract with NHS England to run its federated data platform (FDP), which it says has helped cut surgery waiting times and discharge delays.

The messages – which were obtained under the Freedom of Information Act by Foxglove, a tech equity campaign group, and shared with the Guardian – appear to be between Palantir's UK boss, Louis Mosley, and the former health minister Zubir Ahmed. They span several months from July 2025 to March 2026.

In the messages and a briefing document, Palantir urged Ahmed to "get out ahead of" likely "political" opposition from doctors and vocal critics of Palantir, such as the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, and Your Party, led by Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana. The firm also told Ahmed: "The FDP is already delivering very strong results – but will deliver even more benefits faster with the right ministerial sponsorship."

Groups representing doctors and patients, including the British Medical Association (BMA), have opposed the integration of GP data into Palantir's FDP, arguing there is a lack of trust in the company, which also works for the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). When Rishi Sunak's Conservative government announced the deal with Palantir three years ago, it said: "GP data will not be part of the national platform."

The lobbying emerges after it was reported last week that ministers were unlikely to end Palantir's NHS data management contract imminently, defying campaigners and two House of Commons committees that wanted the company to be forced out as soon as spring. The Financial Times reporting, which suggested the Palantir contract would be extended, came amid concerns that removing the firm's AI technology would be disruptive without an alternative lined up.

The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, last week told parliament the review was ongoing, but said there was "a huge long-term benefit to using the NHS to develop UK sovereign AI" – a sign that the government may seek a UK replacement for Palantir when the contract reaches its next end point in 2029. Bloomberg also reported that Tom Watson, a Labour peer hired as a full-time lobbyist by Palantir in September, recently wrote to Cooper urging her to keep the contract going, saying: "I want to ensure that Palantir UK rises to meet the government's new social-value tests and helps build Britain's sovereign technological capability."

The WhatsApp logs released under the FoI Act show Palantir telling Ahmed that the benefits to the health system of applying its software – known as Foundry – to GP data could include "faster access to GPs … more effective and targeted management of frail patients, and more effective preventative care". It also said Palantir's software platform would "maintain local control of data".

The Palantir executive's name is redacted in the documents released by the Department of Health and Social Care, but Palantir did not deny it was Mosley. In one message, the minister praises a performance on a BBC One Sunday politics programme, just after Mosley had appeared.

"Great work [on] Kuenssberg btw," Ahmed said.

The Palantir executive advised the minister that "the politics [of using GP data] is not straightforward – the previous government ruled GP data out of scope when announcing the FDP. So, as this moves forward, it will be one to get ahead of and explain, otherwise the opponents described above will make hay with it."

Donald Campbell, the director of advocacy at Foxglove, said the WhatsApps showed Palantir "lobbying to hoover up yet more of the British public's sensitive personal data".

"It is appalling to see Palantir pressuring the minister to bring GP records into its platform, despite pledges from the government in 2023 that this would not happen," Campbell said.

The correspondence "shows they knew just how sensitive this was" and it was "telling [that] they made this argument privately, via privileged access to the government", he added.

Dr Tom Dolphin, the chair of the BMA council, raised concerns about "scope creep" with Palantir potentially accessing identifiable personal data in the GP record that could "undermine patient trust and threaten the doctor-patient relationship".

"Patients must be able to seek care without worrying which operators might have access to duplicates of their personal information," he said.

Marc Farr, the chair of the NHS Chief Data and Analytical Officer Network, said: "Palantir appears to be bidding to stretch the scope of its work for NHS England in a way that goes beyond statements from ministers and NHS leaders that GP data was not in the scope of the FDP contract and would require legislative change … As two separate select committees have noted, public trust and transparency is essential to us being able to realise the fantastic opportunities that technology and data offer."

Palantir said: "We've long argued that data sharing can improve the NHS, for patients and taxpayers, and that our software helps different NHS organisations to do that, while ensuring they maintain full local control over their data. We've also always been clear that it is for the government to decide how they roll the software out. These exchanges reflect both of those points."

The Department of Health and Social Care declined to comment.

/education/2026/nov/10/headteachers-cons.headline: NAHT survey exposes toll of Ofsted's new inspection regime on headteachers
/education/2026/nov/10/headteachers-cons.bodyHtml:
The education secretary, Lucy Powell, has indicated she is looking at further changes to Ofsted, after a survey found 52 per cent of headteachers in England who responded, having had their schools inspected under the watchdog's new regime, are considering leaving their jobs sooner than planned.

An Ofsted spokesperson said many leaders had found inspections helpful and constructive over the last year, but acknowledged that others had highlighted the impact on their workload and wellbeing. "That's why we're working with the secretary of state on ways to reduce the pressure felt by heads and teachers, without losing our shared focus on the best interests of children and their families," the spokesperson said.

A Department for Education spokesperson said teachers do extraordinary work and inspections should support improvement without adding to pressures already on schools. "That's why we are working with Ofsted and school leaders to ensure accountability is collaborative, fair, proportionate and focused on helping every school get better, so every child gets the education they deserve."

Almost two-thirds (64 per cent) of those surveyed said the new inspections were "much more intense" than under the previous framework, while nearly nine in 10 (86 per cent) struggled with their mental health and wellbeing while inspectors were on site.

The findings from the survey by the National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) are a damning indictment of the new regime that is the result of a radical overhaul after the suicide of the primary school headteacher Ruth Perry in January 2023.

The changes, which were introduced a year ago, were intended to reduce the strain and workload caused by the inspection process, but many school leaders say they have made things worse.

One primary headteacher who took part in the survey said: "Not sure my physical or mental health could cope with another inspection like this framework. Have been a head for 15 years across three schools and have never felt less able to do my job than I did during the inspection."

A deputy head at an all-through school said: "I previously had aspirations for headship. I will now never go for headship. The stress and anxiety of the inspection has ended that dream … this is the most challenging Ofsted I have ever completed in a career of over 20 years."

A primary school chief executive said: "I'm very tired of the high stakes, the stress, the worry that comes from the whole process. It's on a different level."

A headteacher at a secondary special school said: "I will not do another inspection as head. I will leave before the next one – it made too much of an impact on my personal life – I didn't see my children for months on the run up to going into window."

The general secretary of the NAHT, Paul Whiteman, said the survey findings showed "the unmitigated failure of an unaccountable and out of control inspectorate" and said Ofsted's actions were driving experienced leaders from schools. He said that "another belated rearranging of the deckchairs which sidelines the profession is wholly insufficient".

The survey, which had 242 responses between June and October, comes after teaching unions declared no confidence in the schools watchdog and threatened strike ballots unless significant wellbeing issues caused by the new inspection framework were fixed.

/books/2026/nov/09/m-john-harrison-the-e.headline: M John Harrison, 81, becomes first science fiction writer to win Booker prize
/books/2026/nov/09/m-john-harrison-the-e.bodyHtml:
Eighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award’s history.

Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said that while plenty of previous winners had dabbled in science fiction, Harrison’s was “the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world”. She called it “a historic win, for a writer whose decades of work are lightly worn on every page”.

Harrison, who has been publishing for six decades, overtakes Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019 for The Testaments. He received the £50,000 award and trophy at a ceremony in London on Monday evening.

The End of Everything, Harrison’s first Booker nomination, is set a few decades from now, years after a disaster nobody can properly account for. Set on the Kent coast, the novel sees Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie attempting to survive alongside the looming threat of the mysterious iGhetti: vast, shape-changing beings whose origins and intentions are never explained. At 198 pages, it was the shortest book on the shortlist.

Mary Beard, chair of the judges, said the decision was unanimous, reached after a full day of discussion. “It’s a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism,” she said. “One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible. And the old rules won’t matter either … This is the politics of now seen through the lens of the future.”

Harrison, born in Rugby, Warwickshire, in 1945, sold his first story in 1965 and spent most of the 1970s running the books pages of the speculative fiction magazine New Worlds. Alongside his novels he has written five short-story collections and the “anti-memoir” Wish I Was Here (2023). Climbers took the Boardman Tasker prize for mountain literature in 1989, Nova Swing the Arthur C Clarke award in 2007, and The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again the Goldsmiths prize in 2020. Once a keen climber and fell runner, he sat on the Booker judging panel in 2022.

This year’s shortlist included two former winners: Marlon James, the bookmakers’ favourite, for The Disappearers, and Douglas Stuart for John of John. Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say, Luke Kennard’s Black Bag and Rebecca Perry’s debut May We Feed the King completed the list. Each shortlisted author receives £2,500.

Writing in the Guardian on his inspiration last week, Harrison described The End of Everything as “a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend”, with aliens who arrive “as incomers from another dimension, paralleling the gentrification of places like the UK’s south-east coast”. He admitted to passing on to the reader “some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters”, but said he hoped the issues were transparent – among them “the collapse of rationality that comes with Trumpism and the internet”.

His win marks a rare moment of mainstream recognition for a writer long revered by his peers but at the margins of literary fiction. On BBC Radio 4’s Front Row last month, Harrison said he had been “working for 40 to 50 years to shift the balance, both as a novelist and as a critic”, adding: “Why shouldn’t a well written [work of] SF be considered to be literary fiction?”

Even admirers concede the book is not an easy read. In a rave review for the Guardian, Michel Faber said it “exposes the terrifying insecurity of life right now”, but warned that “it won’t be for everyone”.

The win is timely in the age of AI. Beard noted that the “i” in iGhetti hints “at something digital, but you can’t be sure”, while Wood described the book’s post-apocalyptic landscape as “Large Language Model-dotted”.

The judging panel also included Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, authors Patricia Lockwood and Raymond Antrobus and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu. They considered 163 books published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.

It is the first Booker win for Serpent’s Tail, an imprint of the independent publisher Profile Books, and its fifth nomination. Hungarian-British author David Szalay won last year with Flesh; other recent winners include Samantha Harvey’s Orbital, Paul Lynch’s Prophet Song and Shehan Karunatilaka’s The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida.

/music/2026/nov/09/paul-mccartney-billio.headline: Paul McCartney becomes a billionaire, Forbes analysis finds
/music/2026/nov/09/paul-mccartney-billio.bodyHtml:
Paul McCartney has joined the ranks of the world’s billionaires. Forbes has valued the former Beatle’s net worth at $1.4bn (£1.04bn), making him the world’s third richest musician behind Jay-Z at $2.8bn (£2.01bn) and Taylor Swift at $2bn (£1.49bn).

The magazine attributed McCartney’s wealth to his musical catalog, legal maneuvers, tours and art collection. The 84-year-old derives the bulk of his fortune from MPL Communications, the publishing company he founded in 1969 that manages his own catalog and those of other artists.

The company’s acquisition of copyrights from artists such as Buddy Holly, as well as Broadway musical scores and Christmas standards such as It’s Beginning to Look a Lot Like Christmas or The Christmas Song (Chestnuts Roasting On An Open Fire), accounts for nearly a quarter of a billion dollars. Every time a high school performs Grease or someone streams the song Blue Suede Shoes, McCartney makes money, according to Forbes.

Additionally, as a former member of the Beatles, McCartney receives 25% of earnings from the band’s Apple Corps holding company, which generates about $50m (£37.2m) annually from streaming residuals and sales of vinyl and merchandise. He also makes around $10m (£7.4m) per year from the band’s songwriting copyrights, a treasure in the music publishing that he fought for in both US and UK courts over the past two decades, and the publication estimates it is worth $200m (£148.8m).

The magazine’s estimates for McCartney’s fortune also include revenue from his touring, most recently 79 shows for his Got Back tour between 2022 and 2025, as well as real estate around the world and paintings from such high-value luminaries as Magritte and Picasso.

McCartney is still an active musician into his 80s, with the release of his most recent album, The Boys of Dungeon Lane, this past May. He appeared as the musical guest for that month’s season finale of Saturday Night Live, and performed the Beatles standard I Want to Hold Your Hand for the first time in 60 years in July as part of fellow billionaire Swift’s star-studded wedding to Travis Kelce at Madison Square Garden.

McCartney was also the subject this year of Man on the Run, a documentary directed by Morgan Neville, about his life after his departure from the Beatles.

/environment/2026/nov/10/bee-swarm-nz-au.bodyHtml:
A milder than usual winter has helped New Zealand’s bees build up their numbers earlier and in greater strength this spring, one ecologist says, describing it as a good sign for this year’s bee populations – even as the resulting swarms engulf parked cars and blanket inner-city street signs across Auckland, the country’s largest city.

The Auckland Beekeepers Association is fielding five to 10 calls a day for help removing swarms, with individual members also contacted directly for assistance.

“In past years, it was under five a day,” said Bryan Lang, the association’s swarm control coordinator, adding the team has now dealt with at least 100 call-outs.

In October, a swarm plastered the back of a parked car in Birkenhead for two hours according to witnesses. A woman inside was napping at the time, Lang understands.

“I’m surprised she didn’t hear them because they’re pretty loud,” he said.

A month earlier, a swarm took over a sign at a busy intersection on Auckland’s major commercial thoroughfare, Queen Street, forcing pedestrians to reroute.

Bee colonies swarm during spring and early summer, when part of a colony that has outgrown its hive leaves in search of a new home or extra food, while scout bees search for a suitable dwelling.

“As a beekeeper, you don’t want them to swarm because you’re losing two-thirds of your bees, and right at the time when they should be bringing honey in for you,” said Lang. “And it’s not great for your neighbours either.”

Public awareness about why bees swarm, and what to do if one takes over a garden or street, is growing, with many turning to social media bee-swarming pages and local beekeeping clubs for help, Lang said.

The association’s president, Ken Brown, says bee swarms in the countryside go largely unnoticed, but “townies” are less familiar with them.

“If you don’t know about bees – how they’re only defensive – then you might be intimidated with thousands of venomous insects flying around,” he said, adding that a colony of bees is at its most placid when swarming.

Brown attributes the shift to a much milder winter and start to spring, which led bees to swarm weeks earlier than usual and in larger numbers as colonies split. New Zealand had its third warmest winter on record in 2026, according to Earth Sciences NZ, with other parts of the world – including in North America – seeing similar shifts in bee behaviour as global warming leads to hotter winters and springs.

“Beekeeping is much more unpredictable nowadays because you do have the extremes of weather and the different patterns. Every year is slightly different, but it’s actually even more different in recent times,” said Brown.

Milder temperatures over winter can mean a colony develops a larger brood of eggs, larvae and pupae. Provided they avoid the deadly varroa mite parasite, the survivors emerge “much stronger and ready to swarm sooner”, said Brown.

Prof Phil Lester, an etymologist and ecologist at Victoria University, said beekeepers have also been busy catching swarms elsewhere in the country, including in Wellington.

Unmanaged bee swarms that cannot be captured do carry some risk: they may spread the varroa mite to other honeybees or native bees, and cost beekeepers hives just as they are gearing up for honey production.

Still, it could be a positive signal for this year’s bee populations, Lester said.

“It means they have been able to build up numbers and populations, earlier than perhaps they normally would do … its probably a good indication that it is a good bee year.”
